title: Morgan Stanley Beats Estimates as Bank of America Misses on $1.2 Billion Settlement Charge
excerpt: Morgan Stanley rode a 41% jump in equity trading and record wealth revenue to a clean beat, while a one-time compliance settlement pushed Bank of America below estimates despite growing core revenue.
body:
• Morgan Stanley beat on both lines: EPS of $3.03 against $2.83 expected and revenue of $20.34 billion against $19.74 billion expected, as equity trading revenue jumped 41% to $5.80 billion.
  • Bank of America missed after a $1.2 billion anti-money-laundering settlement cut reported earnings to $0.91 per share; even excluding it, adjusted EPS of $1.08 fell short of the $1.11 consensus, and revenue of $29.96 billion missed the $30.62 billion forecast.
  • BofA's core business still grew: net interest income rose 8% to $16.4 billion, consumer banking revenue rose 4% and wealth revenue 13%; fixed-income trading (down 17%) and investment banking fees (down 11%) lagged.
  • Shareholders were still paid — BofA returned $8.3 billion in dividends and buybacks, Morgan Stanley repurchased $1.5 billion of stock — yet both stocks fell Wednesday, BofA 4.8% and Morgan Stanley 2.7%.

Big-bank earnings week ended on a split note Wednesday. Morgan Stanley posted the cleanest beat among the largest U.S. banks as traders and wealth managers cashed in on strong markets, while Bank of America fell short of estimates after a $1.2 billion regulatory settlement turned solid underlying growth into a headline miss.

Morgan Stanley: trading and wealth fire together

Morgan Stanley's net revenue rose 11.6% from a year earlier to $20.34 billion, ahead of the $19.74 billion consensus compiled by Zacks, while net income rose 6.5% to $4.91 billion. Earnings of $3.03 per share beat the $2.83 consensus by 7%, and the firm delivered a 22.6% return on tangible common equity at a 67% efficiency ratio.

The Institutional Securities group drove the beat: revenue climbed 18% to $10.03 billion as equity trading revenue surged 41% to $5.80 billion on heavy client engagement. Investment banking revenue edged up 2% to $2.16 billion on stronger advisory work, partly offset by fixed-income trading, which fell 7% to $2.01 billion.

Wealth Management set another record, with revenue up 10% to $9.07 billion as clients added $232.4 billion in net new assets, including $80.5 billion of fee-based flows. Investment Management assets under management reached $2.05 trillion.

"Morgan Stanley reported another strong quarter with net revenues of $20.3 billion, EPS of $3.03 and a ROTCE of 22.6%. Wealth Management reported record revenues and added $232 billion in net new assets and $80 billion in fee-based flows."

— Ted Pick, Chairman and CEO, Morgan Stanley

The bank stayed conservatively capitalized, with a CET1 ratio of 14.9% and book value of $68.59 per share. It repurchased $1.5 billion of stock and declared a $1.15 quarterly dividend.

Bank of America: one charge, one miss

Bank of America reported net income of $6.93 billion, or $0.91 per share, down from $8.3 billion, or $1.04 per share, a year earlier. The decline was driven by the $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge recorded in the quarter — worth roughly $0.17 per share and not tax-deductible — resolving enforcement actions by the OCC and FinCEN over the bank's Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money-laundering and sanctions compliance programs. Regulators found that monitoring failures had allowed more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions to go unreported between 2017 and 2022.

Even setting the charge aside, the quarter missed. Adjusted earnings of $1.08 per share, on adjusted net income of $8.1 billion, came in below the $1.11 consensus, and revenue of $29.96 billion — up 3% year over year — missed the $30.62 billion estimate, according to Zacks.

The underlying franchise kept growing. Net interest income rose 8% to $16.4 billion, and the provision for credit losses held roughly flat at $1.3 billion. Consumer Banking earned $3.5 billion on revenue of $11.6 billion, up 4%, as card spending rose 8% to $266 billion and the bank added 200,000-plus net new checking accounts for a 31st straight quarter. Global Wealth and Investment Management revenue climbed 13% to $7.1 billion, with asset management fees up 16% to $4.5 billion.

Trading and deal-making were the weak spots, in sharp contrast to Morgan Stanley. Global Markets sales and trading revenue fell 5% to $5.1 billion as fixed-income trading dropped 17% to $2.6 billion while equities rose 11% to $2.5 billion, and Global Banking investment banking fees fell 11% to $1.8 billion. The bank still returned $8.3 billion to shareholders — $2.2 billion in dividends and $6.0 billion in buybacks — with a CET1 ratio of 10.9%.

Investors sold both stocks anyway

Bank of America shares fell sharply at the open and ended Wednesday down 4.8% at $51.39 on the compliance charge and revenue miss. Morgan Stanley slipped 2.7% to $181.51 despite its beat, extending the cautious mood from Tuesday's mixed start to bank earnings season, when JPMorgan missed while Citigroup and Goldman Sachs beat. Across the group, trading desks and wealth units carried the quarter; credit costs and regulatory overhangs decided which stocks investors punished.
